stem: A logistics company wants to redesign its VPC so that a NAT gateway outage in AZ-A never affects outbound internet access for workloads in AZ-B, and vice versa. Which TWO route table changes are needed? (Select TWO.)

choices.text: Create a NAT gateway in AZ-A's public subnet and set AZ-A's private route table to target only that NAT gateway
Keep one shared NAT gateway in AZ-A and associate it with both AZs' route tables
Give AZ-A its own dedicated NAT gateway, but leave AZ-B's route table still pointed at AZ-A's NAT gateway
Create a NAT gateway in AZ-B's public subnet and set AZ-B's private route table to target only that NAT gateway
Keep a NAT instance running in AZ-A's public subnet and reference it from AZ-B's route table

rationale: Creating a NAT gateway inside AZ-A's own public subnet and pointing only AZ-A's private route table at it keeps AZ-A's outbound path independent of any other AZ. Creating a separate NAT gateway inside AZ-B's own public subnet and pointing only AZ-B's private route table at it does the same for AZ-B, and together the two changes give each AZ an outbound path that survives the loss of the other AZ's NAT gateway. Keeping one shared NAT gateway in AZ-A and associating it with both AZs' route tables is the exact configuration that caused the outage described, since AZ-B's traffic still depends on a resource that lives only in AZ-A. Giving AZ-A its own dedicated NAT gateway while leaving AZ-B's route table still pointed at AZ-A's NAT gateway only fixes half the design: AZ-A now has an independent path, but AZ-B's outbound traffic still depends on a resource in AZ-A, so an AZ-A failure still takes AZ-B's internet access down with it. Keeping a NAT instance in AZ-A and referencing it from AZ-B's route table again makes AZ-B's outbound path depend on a resource that lives in AZ-A, so an AZ-A failure still takes AZ-B's internet access down with it.
